body:
Social media as a means of communication

Social media refers to digital platforms that allow people to create, publish, exchange and respond to information. Social networking services, video-sharing platforms, messaging services and online discussion forums are important examples. Unlike traditional mass media, where a newspaper or broadcaster generally selects material before publication, social media allows ordinary users to act as both producers and consumers of information.

Traditional media and social media are not completely separate. Newspapers and television channels also publish on social platforms, while social media posts may become subjects of newspaper reports. A single event can therefore reach citizens through several connected channels.

How information reaches the public

Information can originate from a government department, journalist, organisation, individual or anonymous account. Other users may forward it, discuss it or change its presentation. A platform may recommend the content to additional users based on factors such as their interests, interactions and the content's popularity.

Agenda-setting means that repeated attention to selected issues can influence which issues people consider important. It does not necessarily mean that the media determines what everyone believes. A subject that receives extensive coverage may seem more urgent than another subject receiving little attention.

Why social media matters for internal security

Social media supports public participation, disaster warnings, education, communication and discussion of government policies. It can also circulate false emergency alerts, impersonated official messages, financial fraud appeals and misleading material intended to create hostility or distrust.

These problems affect security at different levels. A false payment request may directly harm one citizen. A fabricated public-safety warning may create confusion within a community. A sustained attempt to manipulate information about public institutions may affect confidence in democratic processes. However, not every incorrect post is a national-security threat. The content, intention, scale, circumstances and actual or foreseeable consequences matter.

Cybersecurity and information integrity

Cybersecurity concerns protecting computer systems, networks and digital services from harmful or unauthorised activity. Information security concerns protecting information against unauthorised access, alteration, loss or unavailability, whether the information is stored digitally or otherwise. Information integrity in public communication concerns the reliability, context and authenticity of claims circulating among people.

These fields overlap but are not identical. A fabricated social media post can mislead thousands of users without any computer system being hacked. Conversely, unauthorised access to a database is a cybersecurity incident even when no false public narrative is circulated. An impersonated government account may involve both information manipulation and a possible cyber offence.

Illustration

A message claims that a district administration has declared an emergency holiday. If the claim has no authentic official notice, its circulation is an information-integrity problem. If the message directs citizens to a fraudulent website that collects personal details, it may also involve cybercrime.

The democratic importance of trustworthy information

Citizens use information to understand public affairs and make decisions. Reliable reporting, access to different viewpoints and the ability to question claims are therefore important in a democracy. At the same time, protection against deception must respect legitimate criticism, journalism, satire and disagreement. The objective is not to treat every unpopular opinion as false information, but to distinguish verifiable claims from deliberate deception.

Prelims focus

  • Mass media reaches large audiences; social media also allows users to create and distribute content.
  • Agenda-setting influences which issues receive public attention.
  • Cybersecurity protects digital systems; information integrity concerns the reliability and authenticity of communicated information.
  • False information can spread even without hacking or unauthorised system access.
  • Trap: A widely shared incorrect post is not automatically an organised cyberattack.

[NCERT, Social and Political Life II, Class 7, chapter 'Understanding Media', pp. 70–77, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, Contemporary World Politics, Class 12, chapter 'Security in the Contemporary World', pp. 100–110; OECD, Facts Not Fakes: Tackling Disinformation, Strengthening Information Integrity, 2024, sections 1.1–1.2, consulted 16 November 2026.]

body:
What is information disorder?

Information disorder describes problems arising when inaccurate, misleading or harmful information is created, distributed or interpreted. Three useful analytical terms are misinformation, disinformation and malinformation. Their most important distinctions concern whether the information is false or genuine and whether the person spreading it intends deception or harm.

TermCentral featureIllustrative situation
MisinformationFalse or misleading information shared without an intention to deceiveA person forwards an incorrect examination-date notice believing it to be genuine.
DisinformationFalse or misleading information deliberately created or circulated to deceive or manipulateAn account knowingly publishes a fabricated examination-date notice to confuse candidates.
MalinformationGenuine information deliberately used in a harmful mannerSomeone publishes another person's private information to intimidate that person.

These categories are widely used in information-disorder studies, but they are analytical descriptions, not separate offences automatically established by Indian law. The legal consequences of an act depend on the applicable statutory provisions and the facts of the case.

Why intention matters

Suppose an individual knowingly creates a false notice claiming that a government examination has been postponed. That initial deliberate deception is disinformation. Another student may receive the notice, believe it and forward it to classmates. The student's forwarding may be misinformation because the student did not know it was false.

The same incorrect claim can therefore pass through different types of conduct as it spreads. Merely establishing that information is false does not establish the intention of every person who shared it.

Important forms of misleading content

Fabricated content and impersonation

Fabricated content presents an invented event, statement or document as genuine. Impersonation presents a message as though it came from a person or institution that did not issue it. A false notice may imitate the appearance of an official communication, but an official-looking design does not establish authenticity.

False context and manipulated presentation

False context occurs when genuine material is presented with an incorrect explanation. For example, a photograph from an earlier flood may be circulated as evidence of a flood occurring today. The photograph itself may be genuine, while the claim about its date or location is false.

Manipulated presentation occurs when material is altered or selectively presented in a way that changes its meaning. An edited statement that removes an important qualification can mislead even if the remaining words were actually spoken.

Selective presentation, false context and malinformation can overlap. In the information-disorder framework, malinformation particularly concerns genuine information deliberately used to cause harm, such as exposing private material. A misleading claim that falsely changes the context of genuine material may instead be described as disinformation when the deception is intentional.

What is not automatically disinformation?

  • Opinion: A person's preference for or criticism of a policy is not automatically a false factual claim.
  • Satire or parody: Humorous imitation is not necessarily an attempt to deceive, although audiences may misunderstand it when context is missing.
  • Honest error: A person may publish an incorrect statistic and later correct it without having intended deception.
  • Unverified claim: A claim for which evidence is insufficient should not automatically be classified as proven false.
  • Genuine public-interest disclosure: Publication of true information does not become malinformation merely because it embarrasses an authority or invites criticism.

False content alone does not prove deliberate deception. To distinguish misinformation from disinformation, consider the evidence of what the communicator knew and intended. When intention cannot be established, describe the content as false, misleading or unverified rather than guessing the person's motive.

Prelims focus

  • Misinformation involves false or misleading information circulated without deceptive intent.
  • Disinformation involves deliberate deception or manipulation.
  • Malinformation involves genuine information used to cause harm.
  • An authentic image with a false date or location is an example of false context.
  • Trap: Satire, criticism and honest mistakes are not automatically disinformation.

[UNESCO, definitions of 'Misinformation' and 'Disinformation', consulted 16 November 2026; Council of Europe, Information Disorder: Toward an Interdisciplinary Framework for Research and Policy Making, Wardle and Derakhshan, 2017, conceptual definitions and examples; OECD, Governance Responses to Disinformation, 2020, figure 1.1, consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Misinformation, Disinformation and Malinformation

body:
Deepfakes and synthetic media

A deepfake is a form of synthetic or manipulated media that uses artificial intelligence to produce a convincing but misleading representation of a person's appearance, voice, actions or statements. A fabricated video may appear to show someone making a statement that was never made. A synthetic audio recording may imitate a familiar voice.

Deepfakes are important because people often consider audio and video more convincing than unsupported written claims. However, realistic appearance is not proof of authenticity. Conversely, the use of artificial intelligence does not by itself make content false or unlawful. Films, educational simulations, dubbing and accessibility applications can use synthetic media for legitimate purposes.

Deepfakes must also be distinguished from ordinary editing. Adjusting brightness, improving sound or adding subtitles does not automatically amount to creating a deceptive deepfake. A video can be misleading through a false caption even when no artificial intelligence was used.

Possible harms

Deceptive synthetic media can be used to impersonate officials, damage reputations, misrepresent public statements, facilitate fraud or violate personal privacy. In public affairs, a fabricated statement circulated shortly before an important event may cause confusion before its authenticity can be established.

A citizen should not rely only on unusual facial movements, voice quality or other visual impressions to decide whether material is genuine. Such clues can be unreliable. Verification of the original source and supporting evidence is more dependable.

What is a social media bot?

A bot is software that performs actions automatically. Social media bots may publish updates, answer routine enquiries or share information without a person manually performing every action.

Automation can be legitimate. For example, an authorised service may automatically distribute weather alerts. The concern arises when automated accounts conceal their nature, imitate independent human users or artificially amplify misleading claims.

A large number of posts does not, by itself, establish that an account is a bot. Similarly, a human account may participate in a deceptive campaign. The distinction is between automation, which describes how actions are performed, and manipulation, which concerns the purpose and presentation of those actions.

Coordinated inauthentic behaviour

Coordinated inauthentic behaviour refers to organised activity in which accounts or identities are used deceptively to influence public discussion. For example, numerous accounts may falsely appear to represent independent citizens while actually acting together on behalf of the same undisclosed organiser.

The deceptive feature is not simply that people agree or publish similar opinions. Civil society groups and political organisations may openly coordinate lawful campaigns. Inauthentic coordination conceals relevant information about identity, sponsorship or the apparent independence of the participating accounts.

Influence operations and foreign influence

An influence operation is a sustained effort to shape people's perceptions, beliefs or behaviour. It may involve genuine or misleading information and may be conducted openly or deceptively. Its targets can include public opinion about institutions, social tensions or policy choices.

Foreign information manipulation and interference becomes a concern when a foreign state, state-linked organisation or other foreign actor conducts covert or deceptive activity intended to influence another country's information environment. For example, a campaign that falsely presents foreign-controlled accounts as independent local voices involves a different issue from an openly identified foreign embassy expressing its government's views.

Foreign influence is not established merely because a message originated overseas, used another language or criticised a government. Reliable attribution requires evidence connecting the activity to the alleged actor. Domestic actors can also conduct disinformation campaigns.

Three separate questions must be considered: Is the content authentic? Is its distribution coordinated or deceptive? Is there evidence identifying who organised the activity? An answer to one question does not automatically establish the others.

Prelims focus

  • A deepfake can misrepresent a person's face, voice, conduct or statement.
  • A bot is an automated account or program; automation is not inherently unlawful.
  • Coordinated inauthentic behaviour involves deceptive presentation of organised activity.
  • Foreign information interference requires a foreign connection supported by evidence, not merely an overseas origin.
  • Trap: Synthetic media, bot activity and foreign influence are distinct concepts and need not occur together.

[MeitY, Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, G.S.R. 120(E), rule 2 definition of synthetically generated information and rules 3(3) and 4(1A), effective 20 February 2026; OECD, Facts Not Fakes, 2024, sections on foreign information manipulation and the information environment; UNESCO, Guidelines for the Governance of Digital Platforms, 2023, consulted 16 November 2026.]
